analysis.one_liner: Bans meatpacking companies from buying rivals when the deal would create a monopoly.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change a 1921 law that governs meatpackers so that any meatpacking acquisition that would leave the market highly concentrated is flatly illegal. It uses a standard measure of market concentration: if a buyout would push the index above a set level, or raise it by more than a set amount, the deal is treated as a monopoly violation under federal antitrust law. The goal is to stop the biggest beef and pork processors from swallowing competitors and squeezing both ranchers and shoppers.
analysis.who_benefits: Ranchers and hog farmers, who would have more buyers bidding for their cattle and hogs instead of selling into a handful of dominant processors, and consumers, who face meat prices set in highly concentrated markets. Smaller meat processors could also win room to grow.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ranchers, hog farmers, and meat shoppers

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful under the Packers and Stockyards Act for a meatpacker acquisition to create a monopoly, closing a gap where packer mergers faced weaker limits than ordinary mergers. [S2]
It sets a bright-line test: an acquisition is deemed to create a monopoly if it would push the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index above 1,800 in any relevant market or increase it by more than 100. [S2]
Any acquisition crossing those thresholds is automatically considered a violation of Section 7 of the Clayton Act, the core federal merger law, making enforcement more straightforward. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: The largest meatpacking companies, which would lose the ability to acquire rivals in markets where a buyout would tip concentration over the legal limit, and any deal participants whose otherwise-completable mergers would be blocked.

drawbacks.text: The bright-line thresholds are rigid: a merger that crosses the numeric limit is barred even if it might bring real efficiencies or if the market is being reshaped by competitors, which is the standard good-faith objection to per se merger rules. [S2]

Deeming qualifying acquisitions automatically a Clayton Act violation removes case-by-case review of competitive effects, which critics of bright-line antitrust rules say can block deals that would not actually harm consumers. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ranchers and shoppers, the upside is real: four firms process the large majority of American beef, and each deal the bill would block is one that tightens that grip further. The cost is that a strict numeric rule can also stop some mergers a full competition review would allow. On balance this is a deliberately blunt tool aimed at a deliberately concentrated industry, and the tradeoff favors sellers and consumers over acquiring firms.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Josh Hawley introduced the bill on September 14, 2023. [S1]
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day. [S4]
No further action was ever taken on the bill in the Senate, and it received no committee markup or floor vote. [S4]
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired with it. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest meatpacking companies, which keep a market where they can acquire rivals without a bright-line monopoly bar, and the status quo of concentrated beef and pork processing continues.

for.name: Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar meatpacking acquisitions that would create monopolies.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (Chair Dick Durbin)
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to; never scheduled action on it
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred; no markup or vote was ever held, and the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a conservative Republican with one Democratic cosponsor, suggesting some cross-party appeal, but with no votes or recorded opposition the partisan shape cannot be measured; the bill simply stalled in committee. [S3]

industries.industry: Large meatpacking and processing companies (beef and pork processors)
industries.note: The bill would bar acquisitions that push market concentration over a bright-line limit, directly restricting the growth strategy of the dominant beef and pork processors. Their interest in blocking such a rule runs against ranchers, who sell into markets those processors dominate, and shoppers who buy from them.
More buyers competing for livestock would strengthen the price ranchers and farmers receive, which is the core purpose of the underlying Packers and Stockyards Act. [S2]
